claims.text: In Cantor-type high-entropy alloys, the synergistic tribocorrosion response is dominated by mechanical disruption of the protective oxide film as applied load increases.
Disruption of the protective oxide film exposes fresh, less-passivated substrate.
Exposure of fresh, less-passivated substrate accelerates wear and corrosion in a coupled manner.
The proposed material is a cold-rolled Cantor-type high-entropy alloy.
The initial alloy surface has an intact, self-healing protective oxide film formed under ambient conditions.
Applied load will be varied systematically during sliding while electrochemical response is monitored in a chloride electrolyte.
The controlled comparison uses ambient-temperature 3.5 wt% NaCl and compares low-load and high-load sliding conditions.
Low load causes minimal film removal, whereas high load causes increased mechanical disruption of the oxide film.
Protective-film integrity is the structural mediator governing the coupled response.
Higher applied loads mechanically disrupt the alloy's oxide layer during sliding.
Oxide-layer disruption increases wear by exposing fresh material.
Removal of protective passivation accelerates corrosion.
High-load conditions will increase both wear volume and corrosion current relative to the low-load baseline.
High-load sliding will cause a larger open-circuit-potential change associated with compromised passivity.
At low applied load, the oxide film remains largely intact and wear and corrosion rates are lower.
The prediction should hold for Cantor-type alloys in chloride electrolytes at ambient temperature.
The prediction may fail when alloy modifications or treatments substantially improve the oxide film's mechanical resilience.
The magnitudes of the expected wear and corrosion increases cannot be predicted without experimental calibration.
The directional predictions of increased wear and corrosion are supported by prior evidence.
Failure of increased load to significantly increase both wear loss and electrochemical corrosion indicators, or observation that the film remains intact at high load, would falsify the hypothesis.
